Mumbai, Sep 21 (PTI) Amid the Opposition’s demand to declare a drought in Maharashtra facing a widening rain shortfall in some regions, Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis on Monday said “drought relief” measures have already been initiated by the state government.
He said the government would not wait for Central assistance to help farmers facing distress due to inadequate rainfall.
The Chief Minister said formal crop-loss assessments would be carried out after October 5 as required under the rules, following which the state would seek assistance from the Centre.
“There is a difference between formally declaring a drought and implementing relief measures. Under the NDRF framework, certain steps have to be completed before a drought can be formally declared and assistance sought from the Centre,” Fadnavis told reporters, adding that the government has started implementing drought-relief measures immediately.
He said the state government never waits for assistance from the Central government and starts extending assistance from its own funds.
Fadnavis said the state cabinet had already discussed the situation and measures are being taken to address the crisis.
He said formal crop-loss assessments, or panchnamas, would be carried out after October 5 as required under the rules, following which the state would seek assistance from the Centre.
“We are not waiting until then. After October 5, we will technically conduct the panchnamas and seek assistance from the Centre. In the meantime, the state government will take all necessary steps,” he said.
The chief minister’s remarks come amid a prolonged break in rainfall that has affected crops in several parts of Maharashtra.
Opposition parties are demanding that the government declare a drought immediately and extend aid to agriculturists affected by crop loss. PTI MR NSK

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast heavy rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds across several parts of Maharashtra over the coming days, with weather activity expected to intensify in Vidarbha from September 23.
A yellow alert has been issued for parts of Maharashtra including Ratnagiri, Sindhudurg, Nashik, Ahilyanagar, Pune, Kolhapur, Satara, Sangli, Solapur, Parbhani, Beed, Hingoli, Nanded, Latur, Dharashiv, Amravati, Chandrapur, Gadchiroli and Yavatmal.

In a weather bulletin, the IMD stated that heavy rain and thunderstorms were very likely in Marathwada and Vidarbha in the coming days.
Vidarbha region is expected to see very heavy rain on September 24 and 25, according to the bulletin.
Meanwhile, Mumbai was likely to receive light to moderate showers. The city on Monday would continue to experience a mix of cloudy conditions and intermittent rain through the day, the IMD stated.
A yellow alert was also issued for Thane district, predicting thunderstorm accompanied with lightning, light to moderate rainfall and gusty winds on September 22.
Vidarbha faces intense weather activity
Districts in Maharashtra's Vidarbha are expected to experience thunderstorms and lightning, with heavy rainfall forecast from September 23, the weather department said.
The IMD has warned of very heavy rain on September 24 and 25, followed by heavy rain on September 26. Thunderstorms and lightning are also expected during this period.
Yavatmal, Gadchiroli, Chandrapur, Nagpur, Bhandara and Gondia are among the districts in the region that could experience heightened weather activity.
Residents have been advised to exercise caution during thunderstorms and lightning, particularly in open areas and near tall trees.
Travellers should also check weather and traffic updates before setting out, particularly in areas expected to receive heavy rainfall.
Advisory issued for farmers
Farmers have been advised to harvest mature crops at the earliest and move stored grain to safe and dry locations.
Agricultural authorities have also advised farmers to secure young fruit plants, avoid chemical spraying and irrigation during the wet spell, and ensure adequate drainage channels are available to remove excess water from fields.
Livestock should be moved to safe shelter during thunderstorms and lightning activity.

The National Grid Corporation of the Philippines (NGCP) on Monday placed the Visayas grid on yellow alert amid the unavailability of some coal plants and increase in forecasted demand.
In an advisory issued at 2:15 p.m., NGCP said the Visayas grid will be under yellow alert from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m.
A yellow alert is issued when the operating margin is insufficient to meet the transmission grid’s contingency requirement.
The Visayas grid currently has an available capacity of 2,500 megawatts, despite having a peak demand of 2,426 MW.
The yellow alert declaration was due to the unavailability of the Visayas' large coal plants Therma Visayas, Inc. Unit 1 and Panay Energy Development Corp. Unit 3; tripping of PEDC 2 at 1:34 p.m. (Sept. 21); increase in forecasted demand in Visayas; and reduced power import from the Mindanao grid.
NGCP said 11 plants are on forced outage in September, three plants since August 2026, two plants since June, six plants since May, three plants since 2025, two plants since 2024, two plants since 2023, and one plant since 2021, while 17 plants are running on derated capacities, for a total of 859.8MW unavailable to the grid. —AOL, GMA News

Extreme heat fire risk, an exponential threat to children born today in Spain
A study by Vrije Universiteit Brussel and the University of Murcia estimates that people born in Spain in 2025 will endure 7.3 years of extreme weather favouring wildfires, 3.8 years more than those born in 1950.
Rafael Salido
4 min read

A child born in Spain in 2025 will experience over the course of their life the equivalent of 7.3 years with extreme weather conditions favourable to wildfires, according to new research from Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), in which the University of Murcia has also taken part. The figure represents 3.8 additional years compared with a person born in 1950, an increase of 108.5%, in other words more than double.
The estimate is based on a scenario in which global temperature is on track to rise by 2.6 °C by 2100, in line with what is expected if current climate policies remain in place. The study has been published in the journal "Environmental Research Letters" and examines the level of exposure to weather conditions favourable to wildfires that different generations can expect over their lifetimes.
A couple of months ago, the UN highlighted that Spain "recorded its hottest June days since records began on the 23rd and 24th, with temperatures above 40 °C in numerous locations" and warned that extreme heat poses a threat to "health, the economy, agriculture and infrastructure".

"Prolonged heat raises the risk of wildfires, heat stress and damage to economic activity, infrastructure, crops and ecosystems," the international body warned in a statement (source in Spanish).
The figure used by VUB for Spain forms part of a wider study into the future of Europe's new generation, in a continent that is warming faster than the rest of the world. According to the research, a person born in Europe will on average live through 3.2 additional years of extreme weather conditions favourable to wildfires compared with the Baby Boom generation. That is an increase of 84% compared with those born around 1950.
"Our results show that the level of wildfire risk today's children will face over their lifetimes is fundamentally different from what their grandparents experienced," says Rosa Pietroiusti, co-author of the study and postgraduate researcher at VUB, quoted in a statement. "A child born in Europe today will spend many more years of their life exposed to extreme weather conditions favourable to wildfires, a particularly heavy burden in the Mediterranean region."
A record-breaking summer
The findings come after a summer marked by severe wildfires in countries such as Spain. The authors point out that the fires have been driven largely by repeated heatwaves since the start of the summer and recall that, according to studies, some of these heatwaves would have been virtually impossible without the effects of climate change.

By weather conditions favourable to wildfires, the authors mean those hot, dry and windy situations that increase the likelihood of fires breaking out, help them spread more rapidly and make them harder to extinguish. Climate change, driven mainly by the burning of fossil fuels, is making these conditions more frequent and more severe, the researchers note.
This can extend wildfire risk to seasons and regions that were rarely affected in the past, with consequences for people, homes and nature. The study thus shines a light on a key issue, intergenerational justice: those being born now will be exposed for longer to weather conditions that favour wildfires.

"Young people are those who have contributed least to causing climate change and yet they will be the ones living with its consequences for the longest," Pietroiusti laments. "That is why youth-led climate justice movements and legal initiatives are now demanding more ambitious climate action from governments and companies, in order to avoid the worst effects of future climate risks."
A future still to be decided
However, the VUB researchers stress that the future is not completely predetermined. A rapid reduction in the use of fossil fuels would cut exposure to weather conditions favourable to wildfires in all regions. For people born in 2025, such a reduction would, according to their calculations, mean an average decrease of 1.3 years of exposure to these conditions, both in Europe and in Spain.
"The hopeful message from our findings is that this future is not yet written," says Wim Thiery, co-author of the study and professor at VUB, who argues that ambitious cuts in greenhouse gas emissions can significantly reduce wildfire risk and protect new generations.
The researcher also points to the falling costs of solar and wind energy and believes that a rapid reduction in the use of fossil fuels is achievable. "Every fraction of a degree of warming we avoid translates directly into fewer weather conditions favourable to wildfires over a child's lifetime," Thiery says, linking this reduction in risk to the chance for new generations to enjoy a fuller, healthier life.
